If you drive through North Charleston, you probably already know the intersection of Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 feels dangerous. What you may not know is that data confirms it: 629 crashes were recorded there between 2011 and 2015 — roughly one every three days, and more than at any other intersection in Berkeley, Charleston or Dorchester counties. Statewide it ranked second, behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia. Notably, none of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured (Post and Courier analysis of preliminary South Carolina Department of Public Safety data, 2011–2015).

As personal injury lawyers who handle crash cases from this intersection regularly, we've seen the devastating injuries it produces — from traumatic brain injuries caused by high-speed T-bone collisions to spinal cord damage from rear-end chain reactions. Here's what makes this intersection so deadly and what you can do to protect yourself.

If you drive through North Charleston, you probably already know the intersection of Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 feels dangerous. What you may not know is that data confirms it: 629 crashes were recorded there between 2011 and 2015 — roughly one every three days, and more than at any other intersection in Berkeley, Charleston or Dorchester counties. Statewide it ranked second for 2011–2015, behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia; in 2024 it ranked fifth. Notably, none of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured (Post and Courier 2017 analysis of preliminary South Carolina Department of Public Safety data, 2011–2015).

As personal injury lawyers who handle crash cases from this intersection regularly, we've seen the injuries it produces — from T-bone collisions to rear-end chain reactions. Here's what makes this intersection so crash-prone and what you can do to protect yourself.

before:

after:
• 2024 (latest state data): 174 collisions at I-26 and Ashley Phosphate Road — second in Charleston County and the tri-county behind I-26 at US-78 (190) and fifth statewide. No one was killed; 39 people were injured, and 148 of the crashes were property damage only (SCDPS 2024 Fact Book)

5 Reasons This Intersection Is So Crash-Prone

before: Vehicles exiting I-26 at Exit 209 approach Ashley Phosphate Road carrying 60-70 mph momentum. Within a few hundred feet, they encounter a traffic signal. Drivers who are distracted, unfamiliar with the area, or simply carrying too much speed blow through red lights at near-highway velocity. The resulting T-bone collision with a vehicle legally entering the intersection produces catastrophic force.
after: Vehicles exiting I-26 at Exit 209 come off the interstate and reach a signal at Ashley Phosphate Road a short distance later. Drivers who are distracted, unfamiliar with the area, or simply carrying too much speed can run the red light. The resulting T-bone collision with a vehicle legally entering the intersection produces catastrophic force.

before:
Ashley Phosphate Road has multiple left-turn lanes in both directions. Vehicles must turn across 3+ lanes of opposing traffic traveling at 45+ mph. The margin for error is razor-thin — misjudge the gap by even one second and the result is a violent head-on-angle collision combining the energy of both vehicles.

3. Commercial Density on All Four Corners

Shopping centers, hotels, gas stations, and restaurants surround the intersection on every side. Drivers aren't just passing through — they're turning, merging, exiting parking lots, and hunting for entrances. This constant churn of turning movements creates unpredictable conflicts that even attentive drivers struggle to anticipate.

4. Long Red Lights Encourage Risk-Taking

Signal cycles at this intersection are long — drivers waiting 2-3 minutes at a red light become impatient. Studies show that red-light running increases at intersections with longer signal cycles. When a driver decides "it just turned red, I can make it" at this intersection, they're running into traffic traveling at 50 mph from an I-26 off-ramp.
after:
Ashley Phosphate Road has multiple left-turn lanes in both directions. Vehicles turning left must cross three lanes of opposing traffic on a seven-lane road. The margin for error is razor-thin — misjudge the gap by even one second and the result is a violent head-on-angle collision combining the energy of both vehicles.

3. Commercial Density Around the Interchange

Shopping centers, hotels, gas stations, and restaurants line Ashley Phosphate Road around the interchange. Drivers aren't just passing through — they're turning, merging, exiting parking lots, and hunting for entrances. This constant churn of turning movements creates unpredictable conflicts that even attentive drivers struggle to anticipate.

4. Drivers Who Fail to Yield

According to the SCDPS 2024 Fact Book, failure to yield the right of way was the leading contributing factor in Charleston County collisions in 2024. Where off-ramp traffic, left turns, and driveway traffic all meet, one driver who fails to yield can cause a collision.

before:
The intersection's design capacity has been outstripped by current traffic volumes. North Charleston's population has grown to over 131,000 (2.02% annual growth), and the I-26 corridor carries over 100,000 vehicles per day. The intersection's geometry — lane widths, turn radius, merge distances — simply cannot safely process this volume. The crash frequency is the inevitable result of a design overwhelmed by demand.

after:

North Charleston's population reached about 129,245 in July 2025 (Census estimate), and I-26 carries 170,500 vehicles a day between Ashley Phosphate Road and Aviation Avenue, with 65,000 more on Ashley Phosphate Road (SCDOT, 2025).

  • Red-light cameras — Studies show cameras reduce T-bone crashes by 25-30% at high-violation intersections
  • Extended deceleration lanes — Giving I-26 exit traffic more distance to slow before reaching the signal
  • Restricted access management — Reducing the number of driveway access points near the intersection

after:
• Protected left-turn signals — Eliminating permissive left turns during high-volume periods
  • Red-light cameras — A federal study found about 25% fewer right-angle crashes but about 15% more rear-end crashes; South Carolina law currently bars local camera ticketing (S.C. Code § 56-5-710(B))

  • Restricted access management — Reducing the number of driveway access points near the intersection
  • Raised medians — SCDOT broke ground in July 2025 on an Ashley Phosphate Road safety project (Rivers Avenue to Dorchester Road) adding raised medians, high-visibility crosswalks, and better lighting

SCDOT has begun with that raised-median project; until more of these improvements are in place, crashes here are likely to continue.
